::: {.r-fit-text}
Everything glows.
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .mt-4}
You. Your laptop. The walls around you.
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .mt-4}
Most of it is infrared — invisible to your eyes.
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .mt-4}
But heat something up...

## Color tracks temperature

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
Heat it to **$500^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$** $\to$ dull red

Heat it to **$1000^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$** $\to$ bright orange

Heat it to **5800 K** $\to$ brilliant white
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-center}
**The color of the glow tells you the temperature.**
:::

::: {.notes}
1–2 min. "This is the astronomer's thermometer."
:::

---

## 🖥️ Explore: Infrared Animals {background-iframe="https://viewspace.org/interactives/unveiling_invisible_universe/forms_of_light/infrared_animals" background-interactive="true"}

::: {.notes}
~2 min. ViewSpace interactive (NASA/STScI). Drag the slider from VISIBLE to INFRARED.

- Animals that blend in visually (camouflage) still glow in infrared — they can't hide their thermal radiation
- Cold-blooded vs warm-blooded: meerkats glow bright, the tomistoma (crocodile relative) is much dimmer
- Key connection: everything with temperature above absolute zero emits infrared — Wien's Law in action

Ask: "Why does the crocodile almost disappear in infrared while the meerkats glow?"
(Answer: Cold-blooded → lower body temperature → less thermal emission.)
:::

## {.center}

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
Betelgeuse and Sirius are both among the **brightest stars** in the winter sky.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-center .text-xl}
One is **880 times the Sun's radius.** The other is just **1.7×.**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-center}
How could we possibly know that — without visiting either one?
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-center .text-muted}
By the end of today, you'll be able to answer this.
:::

::: {.notes}
~1 min. Let the mystery land. "This is today's question. We'll build the tools to solve it, one law at a time."
:::

## Today's Learning Objectives

By the end of today, you'll be able to:

::: {.incremental .text-sm}
- Explain that all objects with temperature emit **thermal radiation**
- Define a **blackbody** and explain why stars approximate blackbodies
- Apply **Wien's Law** to connect peak wavelength and temperature
- Explain why the Sun appears **white** even though its peak is green
- Apply the **Stefan-Boltzmann Law** to relate temperature and luminosity
- Connect **luminosity, temperature, and radius**: $L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$
- Use the **ratio method** to calculate stellar properties in solar units
- Infer **stellar size** when temperature is fixed but luminosity differs
:::

::: {.notes}
2–3 min. "Today we learn to read temperature from light."
:::

---

## Quick Review: The Kelvin Scale

In physics, we measure temperature in **Kelvin** — starts at absolute zero.

::: {.fragment .mt-3}
| Landmark | Celsius | **Kelvin** |
|----------|---------|--------|
| Absolute zero | $-273^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ | **0 K** |
| Room temperature | $20^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ | **293 K** |
| Sun's surface | $5500^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ | **5800 K** |
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-3}
**Quick rule:** $T_K = T_C + 273$

"Double the temperature" only makes physical sense in Kelvin.
:::

::: {.notes}
~1 min. Many gen-ed students have never used Kelvin. Quick orientation before equations.
:::

## {.center}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Part 1: Everything Glows
:::

*Thermal radiation*

---

## Thermal Radiation

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
All objects with temperature above **absolute zero** emit electromagnetic radiation.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
This is **thermal radiation** — comes from thermal motion of particles.

No external source needed — the object emits because it has internal energy.
:::

::: {.notes}
3–4 min. "Even you, at ~310 K, emit ~100 W of infrared light."
:::

---

## Examples Across Temperatures

::: {.text-sm}
| Object | Temperature | Peak Wavelength | Emission |
|--------|-------------|-----------------|----------|
| Cosmic background | 2.7 K | ~1 mm | Microwaves |
| Room temperature | 300 K | ~$10\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ | Infrared |
| Red-hot metal | ~1000 K | ~$3\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ | Near-IR, dull red |
| Sun's surface | 5800 K | ~500 nm | Visible (green peak) |
| Hot blue star | 30,000 K | ~100 nm | Ultraviolet |
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-center}
**Pattern:** hotter $\to$ shorter wavelength
:::

::: {.notes}
4–5 min. "Cool objects emit infrared. Hot objects emit visible and UV."
:::

---

## Quick Check: Thermal Radiation {.quiz-question}

Which of the following emits thermal radiation?

- Only the Sun and stars
- Only objects that are visibly glowing
- [Everything with temperature above absolute zero]{.correct}
- Only objects connected to power sources

::: {.notes}
1 min. Poll.
:::

---

## What Is a Blackbody?

A **blackbody** is an idealized object with two properties:

::: {.incremental}
1. It **absorbs all incident radiation** — nothing reflected
2. It emits thermal radiation with a spectrum determined **only by temperature**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-muted}
Temperature alone determines the spectrum.

A blackbody iron ball at 5800 K emits the same spectrum as a blackbody tungsten ball at 5800 K — or the Sun.
:::

::: {.notes}
5–6 min. "The spectrum is universal — depends only on T."
:::

---

## Quick Recall: Photon Energy (Lecture 7)

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
Each photon carries energy:

$$E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
- $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J \cdot s}$ (Planck's constant)
- $\nu$ = frequency (Hz), $\lambda$ = wavelength (m), linked by $c = \lambda\nu$
- Shortcut: $E\ (\mathrm{eV}) \approx 1240 / \lambda\ (\mathrm{nm})$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-3 .text-center}
**Shorter wavelength → higher energy per photon**

(high energy) Gamma → X-ray → UV → Visible → IR → Radio (low energy)
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-3 .text-center .text-xl}
**Predict:** Hotter objects peak at shorter $\lambda$ — do they emit more energetic photons?
:::

::: {.notes}
~1 min. Recall from L7 Part 6. Walk through the equation with units: $E = hc/\lambda$, so if $\lambda$ halves, $E$ doubles. The key bridge: hotter blackbodies peak at shorter wavelengths (Wien's Law) AND emit more energetic photons. Students should predict "yes" before you show the blackbody curves.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
{{< img blackbody-spectrum-temps width="100%" >}}
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.fragment .mt-2}
- Hotter $\to$ peak shifts to shorter wavelengths (bluer)
- Hotter $\to$ curve is taller (more total energy)
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-3 .text-muted}
Both Wien's Law and Stefan-Boltzmann are visible in these curves.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
6–7 min. "Two effects: peak shifts AND total energy increases." The two-column layout lets students study the curves while reading the key takeaways.
:::

## Why Stars Are (Nearly) Blackbodies

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
{{< img sun-flare-sdo width="100%" >}}
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.incremental}
1. Stars are **opaque** — photons interact many times before escaping
2. Those interactions **thermalize** the radiation
3. The light we see comes from the **photosphere** — characterized by temperature
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .mt-3 .text-muted}
Real stellar spectra have **spectral lines** on top of the blackbody continuum — we'll use those in Lecture 9.
:::

::: {.notes}
7–8 min. "Stars approximate blackbodies for the smooth continuum." SDO image shows the Sun's photosphere glowing at ~5800 K.
:::

## Predict First!

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
If you **double** an object's temperature (in Kelvin), its peak wavelength...
:::

:::: {.columns .mt-4}
::: {.column width="25%"}
A) Doubles
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
B) Stays the same
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
C) Halves
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
D) Drops to 1/4
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
30 sec. Have students vote before revealing.
:::

---

## Wien's Displacement Law

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
$$\lambda_{\text{peak}} = \frac{2.9 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{nm\cdot K}}{T\,(\mathrm{K})}$$

**Hotter objects peak at shorter wavelengths.**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
This is the astronomer's thermometer:

Measure peak wavelength $\to$ know the temperature.
:::

::: {.notes}
8–9 min. "Wien's Law lets us measure stellar temperatures remotely."
:::

---

## Wien's Law in Action

| Object | Temperature | Peak Wavelength | Where |
|--------|-------------|-----------------|-------|
| Cool red star | 3000 K | ~970 nm | Near-infrared |
| Sun | 5800 K | ~500 nm | Green visible |
| Hot white star | 10,000 K | ~290 nm | Ultraviolet |
| Hot blue star | 25,000 K | ~120 nm | Far ultraviolet |

::: {.notes}
9–10 min. "Hotter stars peak at shorter wavelengths."
:::

---

## Worked Example

**Problem:** A star's spectrum peaks at 290 nm (UV). What is its temperature?

::: {.fragment}
$$T = \frac{2.9 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{nm\cdot K}}{290\,\mathrm{nm}} = 10^4\,\mathrm{K}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
This is a hot, blue-white star — about $1.7\times$ the Sun's temperature.
:::

::: {.notes}
10–11 min. Walk through the calculation.
:::

---

## Quick Check: Wien's Law {.quiz-question}

A cool red star has a surface temperature of 3000 K. Where does its spectrum peak?

- 100 nm (ultraviolet)
- 500 nm (visible green)
- [970 nm (near-infrared)]{.correct}
- 10,000 nm (far infrared)

::: {.notes}
1–2 min. Poll, then explain.

Calculation: $\lambda = 2.9 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{nm\cdot K}\, / \, 3000\,\mathrm{K} = 967\,\mathrm{nm} \approx 970\,\mathrm{nm}$ (near-IR).
:::

---

## 🖥️ Live Demo: Blackbody Radiation {background-iframe="https://astrobytes-edu.github.io/cosmic-playground/exhibits/blackbody-radiation/" background-interactive="true"}

::: {.notes}
~3 min. Live demo. Adjust the temperature slider:

1. Start at ~5800 K (Sun) — note peak at green (~500 nm)
2. Drop to ~3000 K (red star) — peak shifts to infrared
3. Raise to ~10,000 K — peak shifts to UV
4. Point out: the curve gets TALLER and shifts LEFT as T rises — two effects at once (Wien + Stefan-Boltzmann)

Ask students: "What color star would peak at 500 nm?" (Answer: the Sun!)
:::

## The "Sun Is Green" Puzzle

::: {.text-center}
Plug in the Sun's temperature (5800 K):

$$\lambda_{\text{peak}} = \frac{2.9 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{nm\cdot K}}{5800\,\mathrm{K}} = 500\,\mathrm{nm}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-center .text-xl}
That's **green light!**

Yet the Sun doesn't look green...
:::

::: {.notes}
11–12 min. "So why doesn't the Sun look green?"
:::

---

## The Sun's Spectrum Is Broad

{{< img sun-spectrum-green width="82%" >}}

::: {.text-center .text-sm .mt-2}
The peak is near green, but the curve spans the full visible band.
:::

::: {.notes}
Use the figure to make the white-light explanation intuitive.
:::

---

## Why the Sun Isn't Green

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**1. Blackbody curves are broad.**

The Sun emits across ALL visible wavelengths — not just the peak.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**2. Our eyes see the mix as white.**

When all colors are present, we perceive white light.
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-center}
If the Sun emitted ONLY at 500 nm, it would look green.

But blackbody spectra are continuous and broad.
:::

::: {.notes}
12–13 min. "Broad spectrum $\to$ white appearance."
:::

---

## Quick Check: Why Not Green? {.quiz-question}

The Sun's blackbody spectrum peaks at ~500 nm (green). Why doesn't the Sun appear green?

- The Sun doesn't actually emit green light
- Earth's atmosphere absorbs all the green
- [The Sun emits broadly across all visible wavelengths; we see white]{.correct}
- Our eyes can't see green light

::: {.notes}
1 min. Poll.
:::

## Observable → Model → Inference

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
The astronomer's thermometer:
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-3}
**Observable:** A star's spectrum peaks at 580 nm (yellow-orange light).
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Model:** Wien's Law — $\lambda_{\text{peak}}\,(\mathrm{nm}) = 2.9 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{nm\cdot K}\, / \, T\,(\mathrm{K})$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Inference:** $T = 2.9 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{nm\cdot K}\, / \, 580\,\mathrm{nm} = 5000\,\mathrm{K}$. Slightly cooler than the Sun.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-3 .text-muted}
No thermometer. No contact. Just light carrying information across the cosmos.
:::

::: {.notes}
~1 min. Reinforce the O→M→I framework. This is the course throughline: L5-L6 (motion reveals mass), L7-L8 (light reveals temperature).
:::

## Remember the Demo?

::: {.text-center}
When you raised the temperature, **two things happened:**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-3}
1. The peak **shifted left** — that was Wien's Law (Part 2)
2. The curve got **much taller** — that's what we'll quantify now
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-center .text-xl}
How much taller? The answer is dramatic.
:::

::: {.notes}
~30 sec. Bridge from demo to Stefan-Boltzmann. Students have the visual memory of the curve growing — anchor the math to that.
:::

---

## Predict First!

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
If you **double** an object's temperature, its total energy output...
:::

:::: {.columns .mt-4}
::: {.column width="25%"}
A) Doubles
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
B) Quadruples
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
C) $8\times$
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
D) $16\times$
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
30 sec. Have students vote before revealing.
:::

---

## Stefan-Boltzmann Law

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
$$\text{Power per area} = \sigma T^4$$

**Temperature has a HUGE effect on luminosity.**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-3 .text-muted}
$\sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-4}}$ (Stefan-Boltzmann constant). Use $T$ in **Kelvin**.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
The **fourth power** is dramatic:

| Temperature Factor | Luminosity Factor |
|-------------------|-------------------|
| $2\times$ hotter | $2^4 = 16\times$ more luminous |
| $3\times$ hotter | $3^4 = 81\times$ more luminous |
| $10\times$ hotter | $10^4 = 10,000\times$ more luminous |
:::

::: {.notes}
14–15 min. "Temperature is the dominant factor in stellar luminosity."
:::

---

## Quick Check: Stefan-Boltzmann {.quiz-question}

Star A has twice the surface temperature of Star B. If both have the same radius, Star A is:

- $2\times$ more luminous
- $4\times$ more luminous
- $8\times$ more luminous
- [$16\times$ more luminous]{.correct}

::: {.notes}
1 min. Poll.
:::

---

## The L-T-R Connection

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
$$L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$$

**Luminosity depends on both size ($R^2$) and temperature ($T^4$).**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-3 .text-muted}
$L$ = luminosity (W), $R$ = radius (m), $T$ = surface temperature (K), $\sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-4}}$.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
A star can be luminous because:

- It's very **hot** (even if small)
- It's very **large** (even if cool)
- Or both!
:::

::: {.notes}
15–16 min. "This is how we distinguish giants from dwarfs."
:::

---

## How Many Light Bulbs?

The Sun's luminosity: $L_\odot = 3.84 \times 10^{26}$ W

A typical LED bulb: 10 W

::: {.fragment}
**Number of bulbs to match the Sun:**

$$N = \frac{3.84 \times 10^{26} \text{ W}}{10 \text{ W}} = 3.84 \times 10^{25} \text{ bulbs}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
That's **38 trillion trillion** LED bulbs!

Or about 5 billion bulbs for every human who has ever lived.
:::

::: {.notes}
~1 min. "Just to give you a sense of scale — the Sun is absurdly powerful. And that's just one star."
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
{{< img pillars-hubble-jwst width="100%" >}}

Left: Hubble (visible) — Right: Webb (near-IR)

:::

~1 min. The blackbody curves on the right show exactly where each component falls. The gas glows in visible because it's ~10,000 K. The dust is cold (~20–50 K), peaks in far-IR, and blocks visible light. But Webb observes in near-infrared, where that dust becomes transparent — revealing thousands of newborn stars that Hubble could never see. "This is what the physics buys you."
:::

## Same Temperature, Different Luminosity

::: {.text-center}
Two stars at the **same temperature** but **different luminosities**...

must have **different sizes**.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
If Star A and Star B have the same $T$ but Star A is $100\times$ more luminous...

Then Star A has **$10\times$ the radius** (since $L \propto R^2$).
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-muted}
This is how we distinguish **giants** from **dwarfs**.
:::

::: {.notes}
16–17 min. "Same color, different brightness $\to$ different size."
:::

## Worked Example

**Problem:** Two stars have the same temperature. Star A has $100\times$ the luminosity of Star B. How do their radii compare?

::: {.fragment}
Since $L \propto R^2 T^4$ and $T$ is the same:

$$\frac{R_A}{R_B} = \left(\frac{L_A}{L_B}\right)^{1/2} = 100^{1/2} = 10$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
Star A has **$10\times$ the radius** of Star B.
:::

::: {.notes}
18–19 min. Walk through the calculation.
:::

---

## Quick Check: Giants vs Dwarfs {.quiz-question}

A red giant and a red dwarf have the same surface temperature. The giant is $10^4$ times more luminous. How do their radii compare?

- Giant's radius is $10\times$ the dwarf's
- [Giant's radius is $100\times$ the dwarf's]{.correct}
- Giant's radius is $10^4$ times the dwarf's
- Their radii are the same

::: {.notes}
1–2 min. Poll, then explain.

Solution: $R_{\text{giant}}/R_{\text{dwarf}} = (10^4)^{1/2} = 10^2 = 100$.
:::

---

## Quick Check: L-T-R Synthesis {.quiz-question}

Star X is twice as hot as Star Y and has half the radius. How does Star X's luminosity compare?

- Same luminosity
- $2\times$ more luminous
- [$4\times$ more luminous]{.correct}
- $8\times$ more luminous

::: {.notes}
1–2 min. Poll, then explain.

Solution: $L_X/L_Y = (1/2)^2 \times (2)^4 = (1/4) \times 16 = 4$.
:::

## {.center}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Part 4: The Astronomer's Shortcut
:::

*Ratios and solar units*

---

## Working in Solar Units

The L-T-R equation has constants ($4\pi$, $\sigma$) that are awkward to use. But there's a trick:

::: {.fragment .mt-3}
**Write the equation for any star:**

$$L_{\star} = 4\pi R_{\star}^2 \sigma T_{\star}^4$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Write the same equation for the Sun:**

$$L_\odot = 4\pi R_\odot^2 \sigma T_\odot^4$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Divide star by Sun — constants cancel!**

$$\frac{L_{\star}}{L_\odot} = \left(\frac{R_{\star}}{R_\odot}\right)^2 \left(\frac{T_{\star}}{T_\odot}\right)^4$$
:::

::: {.notes}
~2 min. "This is the ratio method — the astronomer's shortcut. No constants needed, just compare to the Sun."
:::

---

## Why This Works

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
$$\frac{L}{L_\odot} = \left(\frac{R}{R_\odot}\right)^2 \left(\frac{T}{T_\odot}\right)^4$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
**What happened?**

- $4\pi$ canceled
- $\sigma$ canceled
- We only need **ratios** — no SI units, no scientific notation!
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-3 .text-muted}
This works because $4\pi$ and $\sigma$ are the same for every star. The physics is in the ratios.
:::

::: {.notes}
"This is what professional astronomers actually use. Textbooks give you $\sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}$ — we almost never plug that in."

**Think-Pair-Share:** Why does this trick work? What's special about dividing one equation by the same equation for a different star? (Answer: same constants appear in both, so they cancel.)
:::

---

## Worked Example: Sirius A

**Problem:** Sirius A is $25\times$ more luminous than the Sun and has $T = 9940\,\mathrm{K}$ ($T_\odot = 5800\,\mathrm{K}$). What's its radius?

::: {.fragment}
$$\frac{L}{L_\odot} = 25 = \left(\frac{R}{R_\odot}\right)^2 \left(\frac{9940\,\mathrm{K}}{5800\,\mathrm{K}}\right)^4$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$25 = \left(\frac{R}{R_\odot}\right)^2 \times (1.71)^4 = \left(\frac{R}{R_\odot}\right)^2 \times 8.6$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\left(\frac{R}{R_\odot}\right)^2 = \frac{25}{8.6} = 2.9 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{R}{R_\odot} = 2.9^{1/2} = 1.7$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-3}
**Sirius A is $1.7\times$ the Sun's radius** — hot and slightly larger.
:::

::: {.notes}
"The temperature ratio does the heavy lifting here. Sirius is almost twice as hot, so most of its extra luminosity comes from higher temperature, not bigger size."
:::

---

## Worked Example: Betelgeuse

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Problem:** Betelgeuse has $T \approx 3500\,\mathrm{K}$ and $L \approx 10^5\,L_\odot$. How big is it?

::: {.fragment}
$$\frac{L}{L_\odot} = 10^5 = \left(\frac{R}{R_\odot}\right)^2 \left(\frac{3500\,\mathrm{K}}{5800\,\mathrm{K}}\right)^4$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$10^5 = \left(\frac{R}{R_\odot}\right)^2 \times (0.60)^4 = \left(\frac{R}{R_\odot}\right)^2 \times 0.13$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\left(\frac{R}{R_\odot}\right)^2 = \frac{10^5}{0.13} \approx 7.7 \times 10^5$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\frac{R}{R_\odot} = (7.7 \times 10^5)^{1/2} \approx \mathbf{880}$$
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.fragment}
{{< img betelgeuse-eso width="100%" >}}
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-center}
**Betelgeuse is ~880 times the Sun's radius** (~4 AU). It would swallow Mars and the entire asteroid belt!
:::

::: {.notes}
"Betelgeuse is cool but ENORMOUS. Its $T^4$ factor is only $0.13\times$ the Sun's, so to reach $10^5\,L_\odot$ it needs a colossal surface area."
:::

---

## Quick Check: The Ratio Method {.quiz-question}

A star is $3\times$ hotter than the Sun and has the same radius. Using the ratio method, how luminous is it compared to the Sun?

- $3\times$ more luminous
- $9\times$ more luminous
- [$81\times$ more luminous]{.correct}
- $27\times$ more luminous

::: {.notes}
1 min. Poll.

Solution: $L/L_\odot = (R/R_\odot)^2 (T/T_\odot)^4 = (1)^2 \times (3)^4 = 81$.
:::

---

## Observable → Model → Inference

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
The astronomer's tape measure:
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-3}
**Observable:** Betelgeuse appears red (peak in near-IR) and is $100{,}000\times$ more luminous than the Sun.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Model:** $L/L_\odot = (R/R_\odot)^2 (T/T_\odot)^4$ — the ratio method.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Inference:** Betelgeuse must be ~880× the Sun's radius. A cool but enormous star.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-3 .text-muted}
No ruler. No spacecraft. Just light and one equation — with all constants canceled.
:::

::: {.notes}
Second O→M→I callback. "We went from color and brightness to physical size — using ratios."
:::

## {.center}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Part 5: Where Does the Curve Come From?
:::

*We've used the blackbody curve all lecture — but in 1900, it was physics' most embarrassing failure.*

::: {.notes}
~8 min. Historical perspective. Students should absorb the story, not memorize the equations.
:::

---

## The Ultraviolet Catastrophe

**The problem (circa 1900):**

Classical physics predicted that a hot object should emit **infinite energy** at short wavelengths!

::: {.fragment}
Classical prediction (Rayleigh-Jeans):

$$B(\lambda) \propto \frac{T}{\lambda^4}$$

As $\lambda \to 0$, energy $\to \infty$. Obviously wrong!
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
This was called the **"ultraviolet catastrophe"** — classical physics broke down.
:::

::: {.notes}
"This was a crisis. The best physics of the time predicted nonsense — infinite energy from a warm object."
:::

---

## Planck's Quantum Solution (1900)

**Max Planck's radical idea:**

Energy isn't continuous — it comes in discrete packets: **quanta**.

$$E = nh\nu$$

where $n = 0, 1, 2, 3, ...$ (integers only!)

::: {.fragment}
**Why this fixes the catastrophe:**

At short wavelengths, $h\nu$ is large.

Creating even ONE quantum requires lots of energy.

At finite temperature, high-energy quanta are exponentially suppressed.
:::

::: {.notes}
"Planck didn't fully believe his own solution at first. He called it an 'act of desperation.' But it worked."
:::

---

## The Model Behind the Curve

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
You don't need to memorize this equation. But it's worth seeing — this single formula produces every blackbody curve you've explored in the demo.
:::

$$B_\lambda(T) = \frac{2hc^2}{\lambda^5} \times \frac{1}{e^{hc/\lambda k_B T} - 1}$$

::: {.fragment .mt-3}
This is the **Planck function** — temperature is the ONLY variable.

- At long wavelengths: matches classical predictions
- At short wavelengths: exponentially suppressed (no catastrophe!)
- **Wien's Law** and **Stefan-Boltzmann** both emerge from this one equation
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-muted}
When you move the temperature slider in the demo, you're watching the Planck function respond.
:::

::: {.notes}
"Every curve you saw in the interactive demo is generated by this equation. Wien's Law, Stefan-Boltzmann — they're all consequences. One model, all of blackbody physics."
:::

---

## Birth of Quantum Mechanics

Planck's solution (1900) required $E = h\nu$.

::: {.fragment}
**Einstein (1905)** showed light itself comes in quanta: **photons**.

**Bohr (1913)** showed atoms have quantized energy levels.

**Heisenberg & Schrödinger (1925–26)** developed full quantum mechanics.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
**The blackbody problem launched the quantum revolution!**

Trying to understand why hot things glow the way they do led to the theory that governs atoms, chemistry, and modern technology.
:::

::: {.notes}
"All of quantum mechanics — semiconductors, lasers, MRI machines — traces back to Planck trying to fix the blackbody spectrum."
:::

## Key Takeaways

::: {.text-sm}

1. **Everything above absolute zero emits thermal radiation.** Hotter $\to$ more and at shorter wavelengths.

2. **Blackbody** spectrum depends only on temperature.

3. **Wien's Law:** $\lambda_{\text{peak}}\,(\mathrm{nm}) = 2.9 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{nm\cdot K}\, / \, T\,(\mathrm{K})$. Hot $\to$ blue. Cool $\to$ red.

4. **The Sun peaks at green** but appears white because it emits broadly.

5. **Stefan-Boltzmann:** Power per area $\propto T^4$. Doubling $T$ $\to$ $16\times$ more luminous.

6. **L-T-R:** $L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$. Use the **ratio method** to skip the constants.

7. **The Planck function** is the model behind every blackbody curve — it launched quantum mechanics.

:::
